findings.text: The opening tells a newcomer plainly what Athena is and what sets it apart, in two sentences. This is the page's strongest part.
findings.source: header, first lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page says Athena's job is turning a request into a code change, but the only demonstration is a read-only study of another project. A newcomer never sees a request, the change it produced, the second model's check, or a cost record, so the headline promise goes unshown.
findings.source: header, second lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: Next steps are easy to find: there is a link at the top and a section at the end with a repo link and two commands. The page doesn't say what a reader needs to have installed before `./setup.sh` (Rust toolchain? model API keys?), so 'what to do next' is only partly answered.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and Next steps

findings.text: The page doesn't say what this command does to the reader's repository or what it will cost. Since the lede stresses that Athena records cost, a newcomer would want that before running it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state-machine description of firstmate, with terms like guard, places-held, exit 75 and close-pending. Someone who came to learn about Athena must scroll through all of it, and the page never says they can skip it.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (t1–t11), and 44 claims

findings.text: The firstmate summary is clear and well grounded: terms are defined before use, and agent and worker are kept carefully apart. A reader who does want firstmate gets a usable model.
findings.source: Start here: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker"

findings.text: These notes are written in Athena's internal process language, not for a reader. 'Recorded boundary' and 'first reading' are never explained, so a newcomer can't tell what these limits mean for trusting the page.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate"; f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths"

findings.text: Saying openly what the sources don't settle supports the page's claim to be traceable. It is a good signal of why the approach matters.
findings.source: Words used first, in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The page doesn't say which repository holds `studies/`. A newcomer can't follow this pointer without guessing it means Athena's repository.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
